Web Teardown
Product analysis · reconstruction specification

Save The Toys

A portrait-first rescue puzzler where drag-matching three identical toys turns a descending shelf into a deadline—and every short run feeds a toy-castle construction meta.

01
Executive verdict

A familiar match rule gains urgency through motion, then earns meaning through rescue.

3

Toys per group

Observed The core action is spatial: drag identical toys together until a three-item group can be removed.

5

Base coins per clear

Visible The first two result screens award five coins before an optional multiplier offer.

2×

Progress rhythms

Moment-to-moment shelf triage feeds a slower castle-building track. That pairing is the product’s clearest retention thesis.

Product verdict. The concept is immediately legible and visually warm. Its best differentiator is not “match three,” but the conversion of matching into a rescue operation under a moving hazard. The build meta gives the reward somewhere tangible to go. The weakest part is communication: the session teaches mostly by implication, while currencies, upgrade cost and fail conditions remain underspecified.

Protect at all costs

  • Direct manipulation of physical-looking toys.
  • Approaching shredder as readable spatial pressure.
  • Aircraft rescue as the emotional payoff for a match.
  • A compact reward → build → next-level cadence.

Fix before scaling content

  • Teach the first valid move with one explicit gesture.
  • Separate game economy from host-platform currency.
  • Show upgrade cost, shortage and resulting state in one place.
  • Make failure and recovery states deterministic and comprehensible.
02
Why the idea earns attention

“Save toys before they reach the blades” is a one-sentence, one-frame pitch.

Idea hook

Threat upgrades a known verb

Matching is low-friction; descending shelves introduce triage. The player is solving adjacency and time at once, without needing a complex ruleset.

Observed

Payoff changes the meaning

A completed group is not merely deleted. A flying rescue vehicle collects toys, reinforcing the fiction that the player prevented harm.

Visible

Meta is concrete

A small castle appears in a landscape after spending coins. The result is more emotionally legible than a numeric power upgrade.

Radar Early public attention is small but fast enough to justify a watch: the tracked gameplay post had 181 views, 22.6 views per hour, five likes and one comment at collection. These are publication metrics, not player counts. Several similar level clips appeared across other channels, suggesting distribution activity without proving organic spread.

03
Product frame

A tiny rescue arcade wrapped in a platform shell and a toy-factory economy.

Audience

Casual mobile-style puzzle players who understand drag gestures, matching and upgrade loops. The toy theme broadens appeal, while the shredder introduces mild peril.

Session promise

Start instantly, solve a small shelf arrangement, receive coins, improve the castle, then raise the target on the next board.

Business surface

Reward multiplication via optional video plus coin bundles and an ad-removal offer priced in the host’s “Gam” currency. Purchase behavior was not tested.

Platform role

Playgama supplies discovery, pre-roll and sidebar advertising, login/save prompts, likes, share and fullscreen. Those are host functions, not evidence of in-game social systems.

Boundary rule for reconstruction. Treat the game iframe and host shell as separate products. The game must run independently; platform login, advertising, reactions, sharing and fullscreen should enter through an adapter rather than leak into core state.
04
Observed player journey

Three short clears reveal the whole proposition—even though failure never appears.

Enter

Open platform page, start the embed and pass through a short host advertisement.

Orient

See a portrait menu with Play and Build; briefly inspect the building catalog.

Prepare

Return to a home surface showing level, coins, offers, settings and a castle CTA.

Match

Drag bears and vehicles together on descending shelf cells until groups resolve.

Collect

Clear the objective, accept five coins and skip the optional reward multiplier.

Build

Repeat across later levels, encounter a coin shortage, then complete a castle upgrade.

Not reached No toy contacted the shredder, no board visibly filled, no invalid drop was intentionally tested, no rewarded video was completed and no later building tier was purchased. Those paths must remain configurable implementation decisions until separately verified.

05
Core loop decomposition

Scan, drag, group, rescue, cash out, construct.

Read target + incoming toys
→
Choose identical set
→
Drag into adjacency
→
Resolve group of 3
→
Rescue + remove
→
Complete target
→
Award coins
→
Build / continue

Decision

Which duplicate should move, where should it land, and which group reduces danger soonest? Even a small board can create ordering choices when shelf motion persists.

Skill

Fast visual classification, short-term planning and precise direct manipulation. The tested early levels emphasize recognition more than deep combinatorics.

Reward

Immediate removal and rescue spectacle, level completion, five base coins, optional multiplier, rising level number and castle construction.

Design invariant: every valid group should improve the player’s survival position and visibly advance the rescue target. If the board removes a group but the counter lags or the conveyor continues beneath a long animation, trust breaks immediately.

Controls and interaction contract

One drag should carry intent, legality, preview and commitment.

ActionObserved behaviorReconstruction contract
Select toyPointer begins on a toy.On pointer-down, lift the toy 6–10 px, add a soft shadow and reserve its origin cell. Ignore background drags.
Move toyThe toy is dragged toward matching pieces.Use Pointer Events; support mouse and touch. Toy center follows pointer with a small grab offset; legal cells highlight.
DropGrouping adjacent identical toys produces a match.Snap to legal cell in 120–180 ms. Recompute connected same-type group only after snap. A group of at least three enters resolve state.
Cancel / invalidNot established.Implement Animate back to origin, preserve board order and provide a quiet bump. Never consume a move or currency.
Open settingsGear opens a modal over home.Trap focus, pause game-owned timers, close by X or Escape, persist values locally.
Build / exitLarge CTA enters castle flow; blue exit icon returns.Back navigation must be idempotent and preserve coins, level and last selected building.

Unverified No keyboard play scheme appeared. For accessibility, a reconstruction should add focusable toys, Enter/Space to pick up, arrows to choose cells and Enter to drop—without presenting that as original behavior.

07
Rules and state transitions

The known rules are compact; the dangerous edge cases are not yet specified.

Level initLoad target, toy set, shelf layout, feed sequence and motion parameters. HUD reads level, rescued/target and coins.
ReadyToys occupy cells; shelves descend or advance toward the hazard. Player input is enabled.
DraggingOne toy is detached visually; destination legality is previewed. Hazard motion should either continue consistently or pause by explicit rule.
SettlingToy snaps; input locks only for the affected cells. Board occupancy becomes authoritative.
Match foundA connected set of three or more identical toys is marked and cannot be grabbed again.
RescueVehicle collects matched toys; pieces leave board; target counter increments exactly once per rescued toy.
CompleteWhen rescued count reaches target, stop hazards, finish pending rescue and open result state.
FailUnknown Trigger, penalty, retry behavior and whether one contact or a capacity condition ends the level were not observed.
RuleStatusWhat can be safely built
Group sizeObserved Three identical toysResolve a connected group once three items share the required neighborhood.
Level targetsVisible Three, then sixTarget is data-driven and must not be inferred from toy count.
Hazard directionObserved Shelves move downward toward bladesExpose speed, delay and danger threshold in level configuration.
Match topologyUnclearDefault to orthogonal adjacency; isolate topology behind a rule module for correction.
Gravity optionVisible “Box Gravity” toggle, uncheckedPersist toggle, but do not invent its physics until verified. Feature-flag the alternate solver.
Overflow / hazard contactNot seenImplement a single configurable fail detector and log the exact reason for later tuning.
08
Progression, economy and monetization

Five coins bridge a level to the castle; “Gam” introduces a second, unexplained layer.

Visible

Level track

The HUD advances from level one to two; the completed playthrough continues through a third early level. The second target rises from three to six.

Visible

Soft currency

Clears show a five-coin base reward. Coin balance is reused on the home screen and castle screen. Exact later rewards and sinks are unknown.

Visible

Rewarded multiplier

A result strip advertises ×2, ×3, ×5, ×3 and ×2 segments with a pointer and video button. Pointer timing and award logic were not exercised.

Visible

Paid offers

Offers display 200, 1,200 and 2,500 coins for 10, 50 and 100 Gam; another offer shows ad removal for 200 Gam. Checkout and entitlement handling are unknown.

Observed

Castle spend

A shortage message appears, then one more clear enables a successful castle action and leaves the balance at zero. The first total cost is plausibly 15 coins, but the UI never exposes that full price clearly enough to call it confirmed.

Unknown

Content gates

Castle is selected in the build catalog; Vestibule appears grayscale and unavailable. Its unlock rule, tier count and functional benefit are not established.

Recommendation: every purchase panel should read “Cost 15 · You have 10 · Need 5 more,” then preview the exact visual upgrade. Label Gam as a platform currency if that ownership is confirmed; until then, keep it behind a provider-neutral purchase adapter.

UI and visual system atlas

A toy-box interface: purple structure, candy actions, wooden play space.

Canvas

Design for a 9:16 logical viewport, centered inside a desktop host. Maintain safe padding of roughly 4% viewport width and reserve top HUD height before board motion begins.

Typography

Heavy rounded uppercase for title and major actions; bold compact numerals for level, target and currency; short labels only. Use outline or shadow over illustrated backgrounds.

Shape language

Chunky rounded buttons, thick colored outlines, toy-like bevels and soft drop shadows. Primary actions use high-saturation fills; utility actions sit in blue circular badges.

Depth

Background factory art stays soft and desaturated. Shelves, toys and hazard occupy the sharp middle plane. HUD and modal cards always win contrast.

Motion

Use springy 120–220 ms drags/snaps, 350–600 ms match anticipation, a readable rescue sweep and a short coin shower. Respect reduced-motion preference.

Audio

Separate drag tick, valid snap, match chime, rescue flyby, coin tally, shortage error and upgrade flourish. Global sound plus volume are visible settings.

10
Feedback, delight and readability

The game’s strongest feedback is theatrical; its weakest feedback is numeric.

Drag

Specify Lift, destination glow, cluster pulse and snap sound should confirm intent before match evaluation.

Match

The rescue craft turns removal into a brief story. Keep the toy identity visible until collection; avoid instant disappearance.

Complete

Confetti, “Done” copy, reward value and multiplier offer make success unmistakable. Coin tally should update after the animation, not compete with it.

Build

The constructed castle is a satisfying persistent change. Pair it with a before/after preview and a named tier to make progress recallable.

Numeric feedback needs tighter causality: the rescue counter should increment in sync with each collected toy; the currency total should animate from old to new; the build modal should expose full price math; the multiplier should preview the actual resulting reward.

11
Retention, social and return loops

The castle is the credible return loop; platform chrome supplies the social veneer.

Mastery

Faster classification, better grouping order and anticipating the descending feed can support improvement if later boards increase density and toy variety.

Collection

Named build areas and castle tiers can externalize accumulated progress. Only Castle and an unavailable Vestibule are visible, so breadth is unproven.

Economy return

Small five-coin clears create a short “one more level” gap when an upgrade is close. The observed shortage-to-next-clear sequence demonstrates that intended cadence.

Platform social

Likes, dislikes, share, login/save and a community shortcut belong to Playgama. No in-game friends, leaderboard, challenge, UGC or referral loop was observed.

Retention evidence limit. The product contains mechanics that could support return, but one short visit cannot establish day-one retention, level depth, economy durability, purchase conversion or whether save works across devices.

13
Growth interpretation

The clearest acquisition asset is the idea, not a verified audience, IP or AI story.

Hypothesis

Idea hook · strongest

“Match toys before the shredder gets them” communicates action, stakes and emotion in one clip. Rescue vehicles and castle growth supply satisfying endpoints.

Counter-signal: the early boards look mechanically light; the hook may outpace long-term depth.

Radar

Fresh distribution · plausible

The tracked clip reached 181 views at 22.6 views per hour on the release date. Similar uploads across several channels suggest active seeding.

Counter-signal: the channels were not established as independent, and coordinated distribution is possible.

Radar

Creator audience · unproven

No established creator following was verified as the source of interest. Five likes and one comment are modest social proof.

Unknown

Known IP · unsupported

Toy rescue and castle building use generic genre imagery. No licensed or recognized IP association is established.

Unknown

AI provenance · unsupported

No reliable evidence establishes whether assets, code or marketing were AI-assisted. Growth should not be attributed to that narrative.

Hypothesis

Platform fit · useful

Instant browser access, platform save, reactions and sharing remove acquisition friction. Pre-roll and surrounding banners may offset that advantage.

14
Development interpretation

The build is content-light but loop-complete; implementation details remain private.

What is evidenced

Multiple numbered levels, at least several toy types, data-like targets, a reusable result screen, settings, a store surface and a persistent castle transaction.

What this suggests

Inference Level content is likely parameterized rather than handcrafted as separate applications. Reused shells indicate a compact state machine suited to rapid level production.

What is unknown

Engine, programming language, asset pipeline, analytics, hosting, backend, team size, production duration, QA process, remote configuration and payment implementation.

Do not overclaim. Visual consistency and a compact feature set can result from many workflows. Nothing in the available public evidence supports a specific engine, no-code tool, AI toolchain or staffing model.

16
Reconstruction blueprint

Build the rescue loop as deterministic domain logic, then hang effects and commerce around it.

1 · Shell

AppRouter owns Menu, Home, Level, Result, BuildCatalog and BuildScene. HostAdapter owns ads, login/save, reactions and fullscreen.

2 · Board model

BoardState holds shelves, cells, toys, scroll offset, danger boundary and status. State updates are deterministic and serializable.

3 · Input

DragController translates pointer/touch/keyboard intent into pick, preview, commit or cancel commands. It never mutates DOM as source of truth.

4 · Rules

MatchResolver detects same-type groups; HazardSystem advances shelves; ObjectiveSystem counts rescues; LevelDirector decides complete/fail.

5 · Presentation

AnimationQueue sequences snap, match, craft sweep, counter, confetti and coin tally. Logic commits before effects; input locks remain local.

6 · Meta

Wallet, RewardService, BuildTree and OfferCatalog operate through transactions with idempotency keys and persistence.

Top-left

Coin balance and settings gear. Keep 44 px minimum touch targets.

Centered shelf columns, toy cells and motion direction. Background is non-interactive.

Danger zone

High-contrast warning band, blades and distance cue. Effects cannot obscure the threshold.

Overlay layer

Rescue vehicle, match effects, tutorial hand and modal stack; pointer events disabled except active modal.

17
Reconstruction acceptance criteria

The replica is done when behavior survives edge cases—not when one screenshot matches.

Host boundary. Game launches without Playgama; an adapter can inject ads, save, wallet and fullscreen capabilities.
Responsive shell. 9:16 playfield fits 320–480 px widths and centers on desktop without horizontal overflow or hidden HUD.
Menu routes. Play opens home/level flow; Build opens catalog; back/exit restores the exact prior state.
Home state. Level, coin total, offers, settings, Play and Build CTA render from profile data.
Input parity. Mouse and touch drag use the same controller; legal destinations preview; canceled drops restore origin.
Matching. Three identical toys resolve once, lock during collection and cannot be double-counted.
Motion. Shelf advance is time-step independent and exposes configurable speed, delay and fail threshold.
Rescue sequence. Craft collection preserves toy identity, removes the group and increments target exactly once per toy.
Completion. Target reached stops danger, drains pending animations and opens result with five base coins for the known early-level configuration.
Rewarded option. Multiplier is optional; declining never blocks continuation; verified completion grants one idempotent reward.
Failure fallback. Configurable fail rule produces clear cause, retry and exit. No currency is silently removed.
Economy. Wallet cannot go negative; build purchase is atomic; shortage shows cost, balance and missing amount.
Build meta. Catalog supports available, selected, locked and completed states; purchase changes persistent scene art.
Settings. Sound, volume and gravity option persist; modal has focus management, Escape close and readable labels.
Accessibility. Keyboard alternative, visible focus, non-color status cues, labelled buttons and reduced-motion support are present.
Persistence. Level, coins, build state and settings survive reload; migrations preserve valid balances and unlocks.
Observability. Log level start, tutorial success, valid/invalid drop, match, rescue, fail reason, result, ad choice and build transaction.
Visual regression. Menu, home, level, result, shortage and castle states pass portrait and desktop-host snapshots.
18
Product experiments

Improve comprehension before adding more offers or more buildings.

Experiment 01

One-gesture tutorial

Animate one bear into a highlighted pair; release control after the player repeats it.

Hypothesis: explicit first-action guidance raises first-level completion without slowing experienced players.

Primary metric: first valid match / level start. Guardrails: time-to-first-input, tutorial skip, early exit.

Experiment 02

Danger telegraph

Add a colored danger band and escalating shelf tick during the final safe distance.

Hypothesis: players connect motion to failure earlier and prioritize useful groups.

Primary metric: hazard-contact rate after at least one match. Guardrails: completion, stress exits, reduced-motion use.

Experiment 03

Transparent build math

Replace “Not enough coins · 5” with cost, balance, shortage and visual preview.

Hypothesis: clarity increases next-level starts from the shortage state.

Primary metric: continue-to-play after shortage. Guardrails: back exits, misclicks, purchase reversals.

Experiment 04

Choice-balanced result

Keep Collect 5 as the primary certainty; present Multiply as a clearly optional secondary action with exact outcomes.

Hypothesis: trust and continuation improve without materially reducing rewarded-video starts.

Primary metric: next-level start per result. Guardrails: rewarded starts/completions, reward claims, bounce.

Experiment 05

Castle milestone preview

Show the next three visual construction steps and how many standard clears each requires.

Hypothesis: a visible near-term goal lifts multi-level sessions.

Primary metric: levels started after first build. Guardrails: perceived grind, store opens, short-session completion.

19
Evidence and confidence ledger

High confidence in the early loop; low confidence beyond it.

High confidence

Directly established

  • Portrait browser presentation.
  • Play and Build routes.
  • Drag grouping of identical toys.
  • Descending shelves and blade hazard.
  • Aircraft rescue payoff.
  • Targets of three and six.
  • Five-coin early rewards.
  • Settings and castle transaction.
Medium confidence

Strong reconstruction inferences

  • Short-level cadence is designed to feed build progress.
  • Early first castle action likely costs 15 coins.
  • Levels are parameter-driven.
  • Optional video is intended to multiply the displayed base reward.
  • Host distribution is a material acquisition route.
Low / unknown

Requires targeted research

  • Exact match topology and gravity behavior.
  • Fail trigger, penalty and retry.
  • Invalid drop and full-board handling.
  • Multiplier pointer mechanics.
  • Late-level variety and difficulty.
  • Building prices, tiers and benefits.
  • Save, checkout and ad entitlement behavior.
  • Retention, conversion, team and technology.
Bottom line. Reconstruct the proven loop first: readable shelf pressure, precise drag grouping, a delightful rescue, deterministic five-coin result and an honest castle transaction. Everything beyond those boundaries should remain data-driven and instrumented until observed.
